glance.why: There is a Chinese saying that heaven is above and Suzhou and Hangzhou are below, and Hangzhou earned its half of it with a lake. West Lake is not a natural wonder; it is a thousand years of causeways, pagodas, planted willows and framed viewpoints, curated to the point that it has its own canon of ten named views. Add the country's most famous green tea growing in the hills behind, a serious Buddhist monastery, and the headquarters of Alibaba, and you get a city that is both a classical landscape and a tech capital.
dontMiss: Walking or cycling the Su Causeway across West Lake
Lingyin Temple and the Feilai Feng rock carvings
Longjing tea village, ideally with a tasting
The lake at dawn, before the crowds and often in mist
A boat across to the Three Pools Mirroring the Moon
Hefang Street for old-brand shops and snacks
The Grand Canal north of the city, and the museum on it

history.story: Hangzhou's fortune was made twice by water. The Grand Canal gave it trade from the seventh century; West Lake gave it beauty, and beauty turned out to be the more durable asset. When the Song court fled south in 1127 and made this its capital, the city became, for a while, probably the largest and richest in the world.
history.origins: A silted lagoon at the mouth of the Qiantang River, made habitable when the lake was separated from the sea and dredged.

periods.name: Sui, 610
periods.text: The Grand Canal reached Hangzhou, connecting it to the north and making it a trading hub.

periods.name: Tang and Wuyue
periods.text: The poet-governor Bai Juyi built the first causeway and began the tradition of officials improving the lake.

periods.name: Southern Song, 1127-1276
periods.text: The capital of a truncated empire, and by many accounts the most populous city on earth. Marco Polo called it Kinsay and said it was the finest city in the world. Su Dongpo, another poet-official, dredged the lake and built the second causeway.

periods.name: Ming and Qing
periods.text: No longer a capital, but the lake became a national aesthetic reference, painted, poeticised and imitated in gardens everywhere.

periods.name: Modern
periods.text: The Taiping Rebellion devastated it; the twentieth century rebuilt it as a resort city; the twenty-first made it China's e-commerce capital.

history.modern: Alibaba's headquarters and a large tech economy have made Hangzhou wealthy and young. The lake and its hills are protected, so the money went east and north. It hosted the 2016 G20 and the 2022 Asian Games, both of which funded infrastructure and a great deal of lighting.
history.whyItMatters: West Lake is the most influential designed landscape in China. The Ten Views are a formal canon, each a named framing with a stele, and Chinese visitors arrive knowing them. Recognising that changes the experience from a nice walk to reading a text everyone else can already read.
visible: The Bai and Su Causeways are named for the two poet-officials who built them, 250 years apart.
Leifeng Pagoda's modern rebuild sits over the excavated ruins of the original, visible in the basement.
The Feilai Feng carvings at Lingyin span the tenth to fourteenth centuries and survived because they are in a cliff.
The Grand Canal is still a working waterway and you can ride a public water bus on it.

historic.name: Lingyin Temple
historic.why: One of the largest and wealthiest Chan Buddhist monasteries in China, founded 328 CE. Working, incense-heavy and set in forest.

historic.name: Feilai Feng carvings
historic.why: Over 300 Buddhist figures carved into a limestone crag and its caves, from the tenth century on. Separate ticket, and the better half of the visit.

historic.name: Leifeng Pagoda
historic.why: Rebuilt on the ruins of the collapsed original, with lifts. Excellent lake views and a legend about a white snake.

historic.name: Yue Fei Temple
historic.why: Tomb of the Song general executed on false charges, still a national symbol of loyalty betrayed.

historic.name: Six Harmonies Pagoda
historic.why: A Song-era pagoda built to calm the river's tidal bore. Climbable, quiet, out of the way.

arts.name: China National Tea Museum
arts.why: Free, well done, and set among the tea terraces. Explains what you are drinking.

arts.name: Zhejiang Provincial Museum
arts.why: Liangzhu jade, Yue celadon and the region's deep history. Free.

arts.name: Liangzhu Museum and archaeological park
arts.why: A 5,000-year-old walled city with hydraulic engineering, UNESCO-listed in 2019. A serious detour but a genuine revelation.

arts.name: China National Silk Museum
arts.why: Free, large, and better than it sounds; textiles, dyeing and costume.

arts.name: Grand Canal Museum and Xiaohe Zhi Street
arts.why: The canal's story plus a restored working-class canal street.

nature.name: Nine Creeks and Eighteen Gullies

nature.name: Qiantang River tidal bore
nature.why: The world's largest tidal bore, around the eighth lunar month in September or October.

food.identity: Zhejiang cooking is another branch of the Jiangnan tradition: fresh, light, faintly sweet, heavy on freshwater fish, bamboo, river shrimp and vinegar. Hangzhou's own version leans on the lake and the tea. It is subtle food, and the two most famous dishes are both about restraint rather than intensity.

mustTry.what: Freshwater shrimp stir-fried with Dragon Well tea leaves and a little of the brew.
mustTry.why: The city's two signatures in one dish, and it only works with genuinely fresh leaf.
mustTry.howLocalsEat: As one dish in a shared spread, in spring.

mustTry.what: Grass carp poached and dressed in a sweet-sour vinegar sauce.
mustTry.why: The most famous dish in the city, and the one most likely to disappoint if badly made.
mustTry.howLocalsEat: Shared; the fish should be barely cooked.

mustTry.what: Cubes of pork belly braised in wine and soy until they hold their shape but collapse on the tongue.
mustTry.why: Named for Su Dongpo, the poet-governor who dredged the lake. History and dinner in one.

mustTry.what: Pan-fired green tea from the hills behind the lake, flat-leaved and grassy.
mustTry.why: China's most famous green tea, and pre-Qingming first flush is a serious luxury.
mustTry.howLocalsEat: In a tall glass, leaves loose, topped up all day.

mustTry.what: Chicken wrapped in lotus leaf and clay and baked, then cracked open at the table.
mustTry.why: Theatre plus a genuinely good result.

mustTry.what: Noodles with pork, bamboo shoots and pickled greens in broth.
Glutinous rice stuffed into lotus root, syrup and osmanthus over the top.

timeGuidance.three: Day 1 the lake, causeways and a boat. Day 2 Lingyin, Feilai Feng and the tea villages. Day 3 Grand Canal, Hefang Street and a tea house afternoon.
timeGuidance.fivePlus: Add Liangzhu, Xixi Wetland, the Six Harmonies Pagoda, and a slow second lake day.

practical.gettingAround: Bike-share is the right way to see the lake and the city is flat around it. The metro is new, clean and useful for the stations and the canal. Buses reach Lingyin and the tea villages; taxis and Didi are cheap. The lake circuit is about fifteen kilometres, so plan which sections to walk. Boats leave from several jetties.
practical.whenToGo: Late March to May is the peak: tea harvest, blossom, and the lake at its greenest. September to November is cooler, clearer, with osmanthus in flower and the tidal bore in early autumn. Summer is hot and humid but lotus season on the lake is spectacular. Winter is grey and damp, though snow on the Broken Bridge is one of the canonical Ten Views for a reason. Avoid the first weeks of May and October entirely.

howLong.one: Sunrise on the Su Causeway, Lingyin and Feilai Feng, then a lakeside dinner. Tight but coherent.
howLong.twoThree: Add the tea villages, a boat, Hefang Street and a tea house. Two to three days is right.
howLong.fourFive: Add the Grand Canal, Liangzhu, Nine Creeks and a water town.
howLong.week: Use it as a base for Shaoxing, Wuzhen, Moganshan and Suzhou.

culture: Lingyin charges separately for the temple and for Feilai Feng; buy both.
Most lakeside sights are free; the pagodas and gardens are not.
Passport needed for museums and rail.
Payment by phone; set up Alipay or WeChat Pay before arriving.
Tea is graded and priced steeply by picking date; pre-Qingming leaf is the expensive one. Buy from a grower, not a lakeside tout.

whatIdDo.plan: Bike the lake at sunrise, both causeways. Breakfast, then Baochu ridge for the view. Afternoon boat to the Three Pools, Leifeng Pagoda at sunset. Dinner at Wai Po Jia.
Lingyin at opening, then Feilai Feng. Bus or taxi to Meijiawu for a farmhouse lunch and a tea tasting. Walk part of Nine Creeks in the afternoon. Quiet dinner.
Grand Canal water bus north, canal museums and Xiaohe Zhi Street. Hefang Street and Huqingyutang in the afternoon. A tea house until it gets dark, then the lit causeways.

quickRef.dayTrip: Shaoxing by rail, or Wuzhen overnight
